analysis.one_liner: Cuts the corporate income tax rate to the greater of 10% or 5 points below the OECD average.
analysis.headline: The corporate rate cut bill sat in the House Ways and Means Committee for two years and never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would cut the federal corporate income tax rate, then 35%, down to the greater of 10% or a rate five points below the average corporate rate of other developed countries, recalculated every five years by the Treasury Department. It would also make any future increase in the rate nearly impossible: if the Treasury determined a higher rate, Congress would have to pass a special joint resolution within 60 days or the old, lower rate would stay in place [S2] [S3]. The bill never got a hearing or a vote in committee [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Corporations and their shareholders would gain directly through a much lower tax rate on corporate profits. Because no spending offsets are specified in the bill, the lost federal revenue would otherwise be made up through borrowing, future cuts to spending, or higher taxes elsewhere [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill replaces the 35% corporate rate with the greater of 10% or a rate 5 percentage points below the average central-government corporate rate of OECD countries other than the United States, redetermined every five years [S2] [S3].

The bill locks the floor in: any Treasury-determined increase in the rate takes effect only if Congress enacts a joint resolution approving it within 60 days; otherwise the previous lower rate continues [S2] [S3].
Conforming amendments would apply the new, lower rate to withholding rules for foreign investors' gains from U.S. property [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally, through either higher deficits or the spending cuts or other tax increases needed to replace the revenue lost from the corporate rate cut. The bill text specifies no revenue offsets [S3].

drawbacks.text: Cutting the corporate rate from 35% to roughly 10–20% would sharply reduce federal revenue, and the bill includes no offsets, meaning the cost would show up as larger deficits or cuts to other programs [S2] [S3].

The 60-day joint-resolution procedure makes a corporate tax increase effectively a supermajority hurdle: unless Congress affirmatively approves a Treasury-determined higher rate in a narrow window, the lower rate stays [S3].

The rate would float with other countries' tax policy — if other OECD nations raise corporate rates, U.S. rates would follow, removing democratic control over one of the tax code's major revenue sources [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concentrated: a large, permanent tax cut for corporations and shareholders. The costs are diffuse: reduced federal revenue with no offset, plus a procedural lock that makes raising the rate back very difficult. There is a genuine policy debate about whether a lower corporate rate spurs investment, but the bill's automatic benchmark to foreign rates and its near-irreversible floor take rate-setting away from normal congressional control without any compensating revenue source [S3].

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Tom Emmer introduced the bill with Rep. Mia Love on January 13, 2017; it drew one cosponsor and was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means [S1] [S4] [S5].
No further action was ever taken: the committee did not hold a hearing or markup and the House never voted on it during the 115th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because it died without a vote, taxpayers kept the current corporate tax structure and the projected revenue from it; corporations did not receive the proposed rate cut. (Congress did cut the corporate rate separately later in 2017 through a different bill.)

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers, who kept current corporate tax revenue

for.name: Tom Emmer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to Ways and Means.

for.name: Mia Love
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill as an original cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no report — for the remainder of the 115th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by two House Republicans and drew only a Republican cosponsor [S4]; it died in committee without any recorded vote, so no roll-call split exists.

industries.note: The bill would cut the corporate rate from 35% to the greater of 10% or roughly 5 points below the OECD average, a large tax reduction on corporate profits. The bill specifies no revenue offsets, so the cost would fall on other taxpayers or on federal borrowing [S2] [S3].
Conforming amendments would lower the withholding tax on foreign investors' gains from U.S. real estate and other property to the new corporate rate [S3].
